The following examples illustrate the
method of preparation of my improved
catalysts. , 55

Example 1

A strong solution of sodium bichromate
or chromate is mixed with sulphuric acid —_
and the hot mixture (90° C.) is heated with g
granulated zinc metal to effect reduction of
the bichromate to chromium sulphate. When
the reduction is finished a solution of soda
ash (5-10 per cent excess) 1s added; the pre-
cipitate thrown down consists of a mixture of 65
basic zinc and chromium carbonates, which
is separated, washed well with hot water and
dried. Itis then made into pellets and intro-
duced. into the catalytic apparatus. -..,.,.

the carbonates depends upon many factors,

ture and amount of soda. ash added. Iprefer _

A solution of bichromate in aqueous sul-

having a zinc negative pole and a carbon

electrolyte eventually contains the requisite
amount of zinc and chromium sulphate for or
the precipitation with soda ash, which follows |
as before. This method of preparation has
the advantage that the free energy of the re-

Catalysts prepared according to this in-
vention are capable of yielding direct meth-
anol of a high degree of purity. If alkali
salts are allowed to remain in the catalysts, or

10 if separate additions of such are made, they
become suitable for the production of higher
alcohol. When, through poisoning, these
catalysts, become less efficient, they may be

- regenerated either by heating to 800-400° C.

15 ina current of air or oxygen, or by dissolving
up in sulphuric acid and reprecipitating the
complex carbonates with soda ash.
